doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

title: Cynicism as high standards: understanding Davern
summary: Christopher argues Davern's apparent cynicism came from very high ideals, and Rowe agrees from planning a concert with him. Christopher says he learned the same directness from his mentors.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Which is I mean that must sound horribly negative but what I think people need to remember about cynical, about what looks like cynicism to people, I think what they have to remember is that there’s a type of cynicism that’s actually only possible because of very high standards and ideals, which actually, ironically, in my opinion, is a very high form of optimism. And I think for that reason I think cats like Kenny were often misunderstood. I think cats like Kenny had such high standards and such a firm system of values, especially when it came to music but when it came to all things, that in the absence of being in the company of people who wanted to engage them rationally and to say engage them rationally, basically share their values, in the absence of people who shared their values and opinions of things, I think those are the people that probably had really a more difficult time. © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

I can attest to that. Because when I didn’t know him very well I thought he was very, very cynical, but then when I got to talking to him on the phone about what kind of group can we put together next year and the detail and the concern he went to: well if we have a trombone then we have to have this and we can’t have just a trumpet and clarinet. I mean he was really, really concerned. I mean this was one night of music, and we were talking eight months away. And he just went on and on about how to make it happen. And that’s when I learned, okay, his standards are partly accountable for the way he is.

I learned a great deal, for better or worse, for better or worse, through all three of those cats, I am my father’s son. You know. And when I say for better or worse I mean I can stir some shit up. And I’m doing it and having a great time doing it but at the same time it’s not — sometimes people feel like you’re sneaking up on them a little bit because it’s hard to always be direct like that. It’s hard to — it takes way too much energy to be like that all the time. So I think you just go in hoping that everything is going to be cool and so if you assume everything is going to be cool and be polite and be cool, that’s great. And then as soon as something goes wrong it’s always a bit of a drag when you kind of have to bite someone’s head off. And like I say, for better or worse I think I learned that from all my mentors. But I miss him so much.
